reference.source: Emery and Rimoin's Principles and Practice of Medical Genetics / relevant specialty textbook
clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive genodermatosis, with the type-2 form caused by biallelic variants in RECQL4, a RecQ-family DNA helicase involved in genome maintenance
The hallmark is poikiloderma, a rash of reticulated erythema, telangiectasia, atrophy and pigmentary change beginning in infancy on the cheeks and spreading to the limbs and buttocks
Associated features include sparse hair (including eyebrows and eyelashes), small stature, skeletal anomalies and dental and nail abnormalities
Juvenile cataracts are characteristic of the condition, particularly historically associated forms
There is a substantially increased risk of osteosarcoma, especially in RECQL4-associated (type 2) disease, and of skin cancers later in life
RECQL4 variants also underlie overlapping RECQL4-related disorders such as RAPADILINO and Baller-Gerold syndromes
Surveillance emphasises skeletal vigilance for osteosarcoma, sun protection and skin cancer monitoring, and photoprotection given photosensitivity
reference.pathophysiology: Rothmund-Thomson syndrome type 2 is caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in RECQL4, encoding a RecQ-family DNA helicase that participates in DNA replication and repair and in maintaining genomic and mitochondrial stability. Deficient RECQL4 function leads to genomic instability, which underlies the predisposition to osteosarcoma and other tumours and contributes to the poikilodermatous skin changes, growth failure and skeletal defects. A proportion of clinically diagnosed cases (type 1) lack an identified RECQL4 variant and are associated more strongly with juvenile cataract, indicating genetic heterogeneity within the phenotype.
additionalDifferentials: Bloom syndrome and other RecQ helicase disorders (Werner syndrome)
Kindler syndrome and other poikiloderma-associated genodermatoses
additionalInvestigations: Molecular genetic testing of RECQL4 to confirm biallelic variants
Skeletal radiographs to characterise bone anomalies and provide a baseline for osteosarcoma surveillance
Dermatological examination and biopsy where skin malignancy is suspected
Growth and endocrine evaluation for short stature
Directed imaging of any painful or swollen bony lesion to exclude osteosarcoma
redFlags: New bone pain, swelling or a mass, particularly around the knee, suggesting osteosarcoma
A changing or non-healing skin lesion raising concern for skin malignancy
Rapidly progressive visual impairment from cataract
Signs of a second primary tumour in an affected individual
reference.prognosis: For individuals without malignancy, life expectancy may be near normal, but the elevated risk of osteosarcoma, most pronounced in RECQL4-associated disease and typically in childhood or adolescence, is the main determinant of outcome. Later skin cancers and the cumulative effects of photosensitivity add to long-term morbidity.
pitfalls: Dismissing limb pain as growing pains and delaying imaging that could detect osteosarcoma
Confusing the poikiloderma with eczema or other common childhood rashes
Neglecting rigorous photoprotection and skin cancer surveillance
Assuming a single clinical entity and overlooking the RECQL4-related and genetically heterogeneous forms
references: Emery and Rimoin's Principles and Practice of Medical Genetics
